RT @pushmeet: Announcing a major milestone achieved by my team @GoogleDeepMind: we have proven key security properties of the machine code underlying the Signal messaging protocol. This is the first time the actual production code of a widely deployed protocol has been formally verified – by any method, with or without AI – and at this depth.

More than a research breakthrough, it’s a prime example of how frontier AI can be a force multiplier to counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats.

Formal verification offers a higher standard of security; however, it’s extremely complex and time consuming, which is why in many cases it’s considered to be impractical. Similar efforts could take teams decades of combined effort. We did it in a month’s time.

Using AlphaProof Code, Google DeepMind's new agentic framework for formal verification that runs on LLMs including Gemini Carbon, we verified the Signal protocol down to the actual code running on devices.  This milestone lays the groundwork for a future in which vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software, ship with mathematical proof that their protections work.

Reaching that future will take continued research from our community. In that spirit, we're open-sourcing our formal specifications and verification artifacts so others can build on this work.

On a personal note, this moment is of deep significance to me. I started my own research journey more than two decades ago as an intern working on checking the consistency of complex software systems. Seeing this grand challenge made practical with modern AI is extraordinary.

I'm extremely proud of my team members: Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger,  Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, and Charles Sutton for taking on this grand challenge and delivering, and grateful to the Signal team for their partnership.

items.content:
RT @MsftSecIntel: Microsoft’s FORGE Lab identified several memory-safety issues in Rust's core and std libraries, including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. https://t.co/2iVeFfAb0H 

The research examines three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Findings include issues affecting iterator cloning, string replacement, and interactions with the operating system.

Using Hyenas, FORGE's research version of codename MDASH, researchers combined AI-assisted vulnerability discovery with technical investigation and validation. They investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

While Rust's ownership model and type system prevent entire classes of memory-safety vulnerabilities, unsafe implementations underneath safe APIs must still uphold those guarantees. The findings illustrate how subtle mistakes in foundational libraries can lead to undefined behavior, and why Rust's safety model remains important even when bugs are discovered.

Read the analysis for details on the findings, root causes, upstream fixes, and lessons for developers working with unsafe Rust.
